title: Faithful in a Foreign House
sum: Jubilees goes back to Genesis 37:1 and follows Joseph into Egypt. Potiphar, a eunuch and chief of Pharaoh's cooks, buys him, and the Lord blesses the house for Joseph's sake. When his master's wife pleads with him for two years, Joseph refuses, remembering the commands of Abraham that his father Jacob used to read: adultery brings a death sentence written in heaven. She grabs him, he breaks through the door and runs, and her lie sends him to prison.
In prison the Lord is with Joseph again. Jubilees passes quickly over the cupbearer's and baker's dreams, which Genesis 40 tells at length, and ends with the cupbearer forgetting him.
readings: Read as a story about law before Sinai

Genesis gives Joseph two reasons to refuse: loyalty to his master and fear of sinning against God (Genesis 39:8-9). Jubilees adds a third: Abraham's written commands, read aloud in Jacob's household (39:6). Joseph becomes a model of the book's chief claim, that God's law was known and kept by the fathers.

Much of Genesis 39-40 is missing: Joseph's speech to the wife, the servants of the house, the dreams and their meanings. What is left is the bare plot, framed by the refrain that the Lord was with Joseph and made all he did succeed (39:3, 39:4, 39:12).

views.E: For the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, which counts Kufale as Scripture beside the Orit (the books of Moses), this chapter adds to Genesis 39 the reason for Joseph's chastity: he remembered the commands of Abraham that his father taught.
views.H: Historians read the chapter as part of the book's argument that the law is eternal and that the fathers kept it. The written commands of Abraham (20:4; 25:7) give Joseph's refusal a legal basis, and the death sentence decreed in heaven anticipates Leviticus 20:10.
views.N: The heavenly books where sins are recorded (39:6) belong to the same picture as Revelation 20:12. Joseph's story of being sold, blessed and lifted up is retold briefly in Stephen's speech (Acts 7:9-10).
views.J: Charles 1902 notes a parallel in the Talmud (Sotah 36b): the image of Jacob appeared at the window and kept Joseph faithful. Both traditions tie Joseph's chastity to his father.
views.W: Most churches read Genesis 39 as the account and may find Jubilees' version a useful early witness to how Jews explained Joseph's faithfulness: by a remembered word of God, which is how Psalm 119:11 speaks of keeping from sin.

echoes: Genesis 37:1-2; Genesis 37:36; Genesis 39:1-23; Genesis 40:1-23; Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22; Acts 7:9-10; Revelation 20:12

settings.when: after Joseph escapes from her, leaving his garment and a broken door
settings.why: To turn her husband against Joseph with a story that makes her the victim and uses his love for his servant against him.
settings.readers: Charles 1902 (page xiii) held that the author wrote to defend Judaism against Greek ways and to prove that the law holds for all time. Read that way, Joseph's refusal, grounded in Abraham's written commands (39:6), is the law kept by a father of Israel in a foreign house.

title: Joseph Over Egypt
sum: Pharaoh has two dreams in one night about a coming famine, and none of Egypt's interpreters can explain them. The cupbearer remembers Joseph, who tells Pharaoh that the two dreams are one: seven years of plenty, then seven of famine. Pharaoh sees that the spirit of the Lord is with him and sets him over Egypt, with the second chariot, fine linen, a gold chain, a ring and a herald's cry.

Jubilees adds a portrait of Joseph as the perfect ruler: humble, fair, taking no bribes, loved by all, so that Egypt has peace and "no satan and no evil." He marries the daughter of Potiphar, here the same man as the priest of Heliopolis. Joseph is thirty. In that year Isaac dies, and the land yields eighteen hundredfold.

views.E: Ethiopian Orthodox readers, for whom Kufale is Scripture, receive this chapter's picture of Joseph as an upright ruler alongside Genesis 41.
views.H: Scholars note how Jubilees presents Joseph as a model official in a foreign court, honest and loved, at a time when Jews lived under foreign kings. The identification of Potiphar with Potiphera and the dated death of Isaac show the book's interest in tidy family and chronology.
views.N: The "spirit of the Lord" on Joseph recalls Genesis 41:38; Stephen says God gave Joseph favor and wisdom before Pharaoh and made him ruler over Egypt and Pharaoh's house (Acts 7:10).
views.J: Charles 1902 notes that Jewish tradition read Joseph's Egyptian name as "revealer of secrets" (Targum Onkelos, Pseudo-Jonathan) and was troubled by his marriage to a pagan priest's daughter, making Asenath a daughter of Dinah in Pseudo-Jonathan.
views.W: For most churches, Jubilees' praise of Joseph's justice agrees with the Bible's call to rulers to judge fairly and take no bribes (Deuteronomy 16:19), though Genesis does not describe Joseph's rule in these terms.

echoes: Genesis 41:1-49; Genesis 41:16; Genesis 41:38; Genesis 41:45; Genesis 35:28-29; Deuteronomy 16:19; Acts 7:10

settings.what: Joseph explains Pharaoh's dreams and gives advice
settings.when: when Joseph is brought from prison to the king
settings.why: To tell Pharaoh what the two dreams mean and how to save the land: store food in every city during the years of plenty.
settings.readers: The scene puts a son of Jacob before a foreign king as his wise counselor. Readers who knew Daniel could see the likeness (Daniel 2); the comparison is the site's, not the book's.

settings.why: To declare that no one is as wise as Joseph, because the spirit of the Lord is with him, and so to justify setting a foreign slave over Egypt.

title: Judah and Tamar
sum: In the middle of the years of plenty, Judah takes Tamar, an Aramean woman, as wife for his son Er. Er hates her because he wants a Canaanite wife like his mother, and the Lord puts him to death. Onan refuses to give his brother a son and dies too. Judah's Canaanite wife Bedsuel keeps Shelah from Tamar. Tamar veils herself by the road to Timnah, Judah takes her for a prostitute and gives her his ring, necklace and staff as a pledge, and she conceives. When Judah orders her burned, she sends the pledge, and he confesses that she is more in the right.

Jubilees then adds what Genesis 38 does not have: Judah's grief and repentance, the angels' word in a dream that he is forgiven, and a law for Israel that a man who lies with his daughter-in-law or mother-in-law is to be burned with the woman. Judah's line survives because Er and Onan never truly lay with Tamar.
readings: Read as a defense of Judah

Jubilees moves the blame for Tamar's long wait from Judah to his Canaanite wife (41:7), drops his own confession that he never gave her to Shelah (Genesis 38:26), and shows him repenting and forgiven (41:23-24). The tribe of kings is cleared as far as the story allows.

Like many chapters of Jubilees, this one turns a story into a law: burning for sexual union with a daughter-in-law or mother-in-law (41:25-26), set beside Leviticus 18 and 20. The fathers' sins become the occasion for Moses' law.

views.E: For the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, which holds Kufale as Scripture, this chapter gives Genesis 38 a fuller moral frame: Judah's sin is named, his repentance and forgiveness are told, and the law against such unions is declared.
views.H: Historians see here several of the book's concerns at once: hostility to marriage with Canaanites (Er's sin, Bedsuel's blame), the honor of Judah, and severe laws on sexual purity enforced by burning (compare 20:4; 30:7). Charles 1902 notes how close the chapter is to the Testament of Judah 10-19.
views.N: Tamar is one of the women named in Jesus' genealogy (Matthew 1:3). Jubilees' theme of sin forgiven because it was done in ignorance and repented of is close to Paul's words in 1 Timothy 1:13.
views.J: Charles 1902 reports that Rabbi Meir (Genesis Rabbah 85) made Tamar a priest's daughter, explaining the sentence of burning by Leviticus 21:9; Jubilees explains it instead by Abraham's command (41:28).
views.W: Most churches read Genesis 38 on its own terms, where Judah's fault is plain and Tamar is declared more in the right. They can value Jubilees as an early Jewish attempt to explain the story, while noting that it softens Judah's guilt and adds laws not found in the Bible.

deep.b:
Set side by side with Genesis 38, Jubilees' version shows a pattern. Tamar gets a good origin, "from the daughters of Aram" (41:1). Er's evil is given a cause, his wish for a Canaanite wife (41:2). The blame for withholding Shelah moves from Judah to his Canaanite wife (41:7; compare Genesis 38:11, 14). Judah offers his pledge himself (41:11), and his reason for Tamar's righteousness, "because I never gave her to my son Shelah" (Genesis 38:26), disappears. Then come additions: Tamar is never given to Shelah (41:20), Judah repents and is forgiven (41:23-25), and the angel gives Moses a law (41:25-26).

The Testament of Judah, quoted at length in Charles 1902 (pages 228-231), shares many of these details: Tamar from Mesopotamia, Er and Onan led by their Canaanite mother, Judah's later repentance and his plea of ignorance. Charles thought Jubilees and the Testaments drew on the same traditions.

The law of Moses sets death for sleeping with a daughter-in-law (Leviticus 20:12) and burning for taking a woman and her mother (Leviticus 20:14). It sets burning for a priest's daughter who becomes a prostitute (Leviticus 21:9). Jubilees sets burning for both the daughter-in-law and mother-in-law cases, man and woman alike (41:25-26), and grounds Judah's sentence on Tamar in Abraham's command (20:4; 41:28). The angel promises that keeping this law will turn God's anger away from Israel.

echoes: Genesis 38:1-30; Leviticus 18:15; Leviticus 20:12; Leviticus 20:14; Leviticus 21:9; Deuteronomy 25:5-10; Ruth 4:12; Ruth 4:18-22; Matthew 1:3; 1 Timothy 1:13

settings.why: To have Onan do a brother-in-law's duty and give the dead Er a son.

settings.when: after Judah has mourned and pleaded with the Lord over his sin
settings.why: To tell Judah he is forgiven, because he repented and did not repeat the sin.
settings.readers: The angel tells this to Moses, and through him to Israel: the lesson is stated in the text itself, that a father of the nation sinned gravely, turned back, and was forgiven (41:23-25).

settings.what: The law against lying with a mother-in-law or daughter-in-law
settings.to: Moses on Mount Sinai, to command the Israelites
settings.when: as part of the angel's retelling of Judah's story
settings.why: To bind every Israelite man and woman, in the land and in every generation, to keep this kind of uncleanness out of Israel, on pain of burning, so that God's anger would not fall on the whole people.
settings.readers: The law is addressed to every later generation of Israel: Moses is told to command the Israelites (41:26). It adds to Leviticus 18 and 20 and shows the book's strict view of sexual purity.

settings.when: closing the story of Judah and Tamar
settings.why: To explain to Moses why the line of Judah, the tribe of kings, was not cut off: Tamar's marriages to his sons were never consummated, and Judah had acted in honest zeal for Abraham's law.

title: Grain in Egypt
sum: The famine begins in year 2171: no rain falls, and only Egypt has food. Jacob sends ten sons to buy grain but keeps Benjamin home. Joseph knows them, calls them spies, keeps Simeon, and sends the rest home with their gold in their sacks. Jacob refuses to let Benjamin go. When the famine deepens, Reuben offers his two sons as pledge, and Jacob refuses; Judah offers to carry the guilt himself, and Jacob agrees.

In Egypt Joseph sees Benjamin, frees Simeon, and feasts the brothers, giving Benjamin seven times as much. Then he plans a test to learn whether the brothers have peaceful thoughts toward one another, and has his silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack.

views.E: Ethiopian Orthodox readers, for whom Kufale is Scripture, read here a shorter account of Genesis 42-44 that makes Joseph's purpose plain: to test whether his brothers were at peace with one another.
views.H: Historians note the book's habit of giving reasons Genesis leaves out: no rain as the cause of the famine, Egyptians storing their own grain, Joseph's motive for the test. Judah's offer is set beside Reuben's and preferred, in keeping with the book's honor for Judah.
views.N: Stephen tells of the famine and the brothers' two journeys in Acts 7:11-13. The theme of brothers at peace with one another, which Jubilees makes Joseph's test, runs through the New Testament's call to love one another (1 John 3:11-12).
views.J: Jewish retellings, like Jubilees, often asked why Joseph treated his brothers harshly; Jubilees' answer is that he was testing their unity, not taking revenge.
views.W: Most churches read Genesis 42-44 itself, where Joseph's motives are left for the reader to weigh. Jubilees' explanation is one early reading among several.

settings.when: when they report that Simeon is held until they bring Benjamin
settings.why: To refuse to send Benjamin, the only son left of Rachel, and to hold his sons to account for the losses he has suffered.

settings.when: as the famine grows worse and they must go back to Egypt
settings.why: To win Jacob's consent to send Benjamin: Reuben by offering his two sons' lives, Judah by taking the guilt on himself for life.
settings.readers: Setting Judah's pledge above Reuben's fits the book's honor for the tribe of Judah (31:18).

title: The Cup and the Reunion
sum: Joseph's steward overtakes the brothers and finds the silver cup in Benjamin's sack. They return and bow before Joseph, who says he will keep Benjamin as a slave. Judah pleads: the boy's mother had two sons, one is lost, their father's life is bound up with this boy, and Judah stood as guarantor; let him be the slave instead.

Joseph sees that their hearts are united for good. He tells them who he is, speaks to them in Hebrew, weeps, and sends them to bring their father, explaining that the Lord sent him ahead to keep many people alive. At Pharaoh's order he sends carts, clothes, silver and grain. Jacob does not believe at first, but when he sees the carts his spirit revives: it is enough that Joseph is alive.

views.E: For the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, which counts Kufale as Scripture, the reunion completes the testing of the brothers, and Joseph's words teach that God turned evil into the saving of many lives.
views.H: Scholars point to what Jubilees removes, above all Joseph's divining cup (Genesis 44:5, 15), which the law forbids. At 43:10 Charles 1902 (page 236) says only that the change may be deliberate; in his introduction (page xiii) he describes the book in general as an expanded Genesis from which "dogmatically offensive elements" are removed. Hebrew as the language Joseph speaks fits the book's view of Hebrew as the language of creation (12:25-26).
views.N: Joseph's words that God sent him ahead to save lives (43:18; Genesis 50:20) belong with Romans 8:28 in Christian reflection on providence. Stephen tells that the second time Joseph made himself known to his brothers (Acts 7:13).
views.J: Charles 1902 notes that Genesis Rabbah 93 also has Joseph speak Hebrew to his brothers, a detail shared with Jubilees.
views.W: Most churches read the reunion in Genesis 44-45 and can see in Jubilees an early witness to how carefully Jewish readers handled the divining cup and the brothers' guilt.

settings.what: The steward's charge and the brothers' answer
settings.when: on the road out of the city, early in the morning
settings.why: To spring Joseph's test: to accuse the brothers of theft so that Benjamin can be held and their loyalty to him tried.

settings.to: Joseph, whom he takes for an Egyptian lord
settings.when: after the cup is found and Joseph says he will keep Benjamin
settings.why: To move the lord to mercy for an old father and to offer himself as a slave in Benjamin's place, keeping the pledge he made to Jacob (42:19).
settings.readers: For readers who knew Genesis 37, Judah's offer to be a slave in Benjamin's place answers his earlier plan to sell Joseph (Genesis 37:26-27).

settings.when: after Judah's plea shows that their hearts are united
settings.why: To end their fear and grief, explain that the Lord sent him ahead to save many people, and have them bring Jacob and the households down to Egypt.

title: Jacob Goes Down to Egypt
sum: Jacob sets out on the first day of the third month and offers sacrifice at the Well of the Oath, Beersheba. Remembering his dream at Bethel, he is afraid to leave Canaan and waits seven days for a vision. He keeps the harvest festival of first fruits with old grain, since nothing grows. On the sixteenth the Lord appears: "Do not fear going down to Egypt." God promises to go with him, make him a great nation, bring him up again, and that Joseph will close his eyes.

The family sets out in carts, and Judah goes ahead to Goshen. Then comes the list of those who went down: seventy persons, counting Jacob. The list differs from Genesis 46 in many details, with five sons each for Dan and Naphtali, and it ends with Er and Onan, who died in Canaan and are counted among the seventy nations.

views.E: Ethiopian Orthodox readers, who keep Kufale as Scripture, read here that Jacob kept the feast of first fruits even in famine and went down only after God spoke to him.
views.H: Historians note the exact dating: Jacob keeps the Feast of Weeks on the fifteenth of the third month, the date the book's calendar sets (Charles 1902). The list of the seventy is reworked so that the count includes Jacob, and its names often follow the Greek Genesis or the Samaritan text.
views.N: Stephen says Jacob's clan numbered seventy-five (Acts 7:14), the Septuagint's figure; Jubilees, with the Hebrew of Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5, counts seventy.
views.J: Charles 1902 notes that the Targum called Pseudo-Jonathan and the Talmud (Bava Batra 143b) also gave Dan more than one son, as Jubilees does. Jubilees' Feast of Weeks on a fixed date, the fifteenth of the third month, belongs to its 364-day calendar.
views.W: Most churches read the list in Genesis 46 and the Hebrew count of seventy. They can use Jubilees as early evidence that Jews counted the seventy in more than one way.

deep.b:
Genesis 46:26-27 counts sixty-six descendants who went down with Jacob, then seventy with Joseph and his two sons and Jacob. Jubilees counts differently. Charles 1902 (page 239) lays out its figures: Leah's side 29 (44:18), Zilpah's 14 (44:22), Rachel's 14 (44:26), Bilhah's 12 (44:32 with 44:26), which comes to 69, and Jacob makes 70. To reach this, Jubilees leaves out Er and Onan, Perez's two sons, Asher's two grandsons and Dinah, and gives Dan and Naphtali five sons each.

The Greek Genesis and Exodus have seventy-five (Genesis 46:27; Exodus 1:5), and Stephen follows the Greek in Acts 7:14. Jubilees agrees with the Hebrew total but builds it differently. Seventy also echoes the seventy nations of the world (44:34; Genesis 10).

echoes: Genesis 46:1-28; Genesis 21:31; Genesis 28:15; Exodus 1:1-5; Exodus 23:16; Exodus 34:22; Deuteronomy 10:22; Acts 7:14-15

settings.what: God's word to Jacob at the Well of the Oath
settings.to: Jacob, after seven days of waiting
settings.when: on the sixteenth of the third month, the day after the harvest festival
settings.why: To take away Jacob's fear of leaving the promised land: God will go with him, make him a great nation, bring him back, and let Joseph be with him at his death.
settings.readers: The vision is dated the day after the Feast of Weeks (44:1-5), so the promise to go down with Jacob is tied to the festival calendar the book teaches (6:17).

title: Jacob's Last Years
sum: Jacob reaches Goshen on the first day of the fourth month. Joseph meets him and weeps on his neck, and Jacob blesses God, saying the vision at Bethel has come true. The whole family eats together, and Jacob rejoices that all twelve sons are safe. Joseph settles them in Goshen and Rameses and feeds them through the famine. He buys all Egypt for Pharaoh with food; when the Nile floods again in the eighth year, he gives seed and sets the rule of a fifth for the king.

Jacob lives seventeen years in Egypt and dies at a hundred and forty-seven, exactly three jubilees. He blesses his sons, tells them what will happen in Egypt and in the last days, gives Joseph two portions, and is buried with Abraham in the double cave at Hebron. Last of all he gives his books and his fathers' books to Levi, to keep and renew.

views.E: For the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, which counts Kufale as Scripture, the chapter closes the life of Jacob and ends with the handing of the fathers' books to Levi, the priestly son.
views.H: Historians often point to 45:16 for the book's own claim to authority: the fathers' writings were kept by Levi's line. Charles 1902 inferred from it that the author was a descendant of Levi and probably a priest. Jacob's hundred and forty-seven years as three jubilees show how neatly Genesis's numbers fit the book's calendar.
views.N: Hebrews 11:21 remembers Jacob blessing Joseph's sons as he was dying; Stephen says Jacob died in Egypt and that the fathers were buried at Shechem (Acts 7:15-16), where Jubilees, with Genesis, has Hebron.
views.J: Jubilees' idea of books handed down in the priestly line (45:16; 10:14) can be set beside the Mishnah's chain of tradition: "Moses received the Torah at Sinai and transmitted it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, and the elders to the prophets" (Mishnah Avot 1:1, in the English on Sefaria).
views.W: Most churches read Genesis 46-50 and find no books of the patriarchs in Scripture. They can read 45:16 as Jubilees' claim about its own sources, to be weighed rather than assumed.

deep.b:
Jubilees imagines a written tradition older than Moses. Enoch writes down what he learned (4:17-19), Noah writes a book of healing and gives his books to Shem (10:13-14), Jacob reads Abraham's words to his household (39:6), and now Jacob gives "all his books, and the books of his fathers" to Levi (45:16). "To this day" is the angel speaking to Moses; Moses, a descendant of Levi, is the heir of that library.

The claim supports the book's authority: what it tells, beyond Genesis, comes from writings kept by the priests. Charles 1902 (page 244) drew the natural inference that the author was a priest of Levi's line. The 66 books also give the priests charge of the law (Deuteronomy 31:9; Malachi 2:7), but they speak of no writings from the patriarchs.

echoes: Genesis 46:28-30; Genesis 47:9-28; Genesis 48:22; Genesis 49:1-33; Genesis 50:1-14; Deuteronomy 21:17; Deuteronomy 31:9; Malachi 2:7; Acts 7:15-16; Hebrews 11:21

settings.to: Joseph, and through him to God
settings.when: when Joseph meets him in Goshen
settings.why: To praise the God of Abraham and Isaac, who kept his mercy toward Jacob, and to declare the Bethel vision true now that he has seen Joseph alive.
To bless his sons, tell them what would happen to them in Egypt and in the last days, and give Joseph the firstborn's double portion.
settings.readers: The verse tells readers that the future of the tribes, to the last days, was foretold to the fathers, without repeating Genesis 49.

settings.when: at the end of Jacob's life
settings.why: To place the family's writings in the keeping of the priestly son, to be preserved and copied for his descendants.
settings.readers: The verse claims a priestly source for the book's traditions: Charles 1902 (page 244) inferred that the author was "a descendant of Levi, and probably a priest."
